eligibility: McGraw Hill identifies a one- or two-semester advanced analysis text. The contents teach integration, measure, Banach spaces and complex analysis as a cumulative technical course.
reason: Its main purpose is training in mathematical analysis; the unification of real and complex methods does not change that instructional structure.

eligibility: The publisher describes a Harvard statistics course text with chapter exercises, R simulations, sample examinations and an instructor solutions manual.
reason: Intuitive explanations and applications support probability instruction; they do not turn the book into narrative nonfiction.

eligibility: Taboga's own Statlect book page calls this a textbook for self-study, built from lectures, worked examples, proofs and solved exercises.
reason: The work teaches probability and statistical procedures. Self-study is expressly covered by H2.

eligibility: Cengage identifies Casella and Berger's Statistical Inference as a first-year graduate statistics text, developing inference and procedures from probability foundations.
reason: The distinctive author pair resolves the source's mistaken title 'mathematical statistics'; the identified work is a technical course text.

eligibility: Cambridge's description and Jaynes's preface target advanced mathematical readers applying inference. The book develops probability mathematics with exercises, problems and technical applications, and is intended for graduate data-analysis courses.
reason: Its sustained Bayesian argument and broad applications do not remove its primary role as a technical treatment and instructional reference for inference.

eligibility: Cox's author page describes the technical development of class fields, modular functions and complex multiplication; editions include extensive exercises and complete solutions.
reason: The historical motivation serves systematic mathematical method development. This is a specialist number-theory text, not a general history of Fermat.

eligibility: The London Mathematical Society identifies these as lectures from an instructional conference and a standard course text in algebraic number theory.
reason: The target is aspiring algebraic number theorists and technical class-field training; landmark research contributions do not override H2.

eligibility: Cambridge calls it a second course in Galois theory for advanced undergraduates and beginning graduate students, with exercises and a progression through local fields, Brauer groups and cohomology.
reason: The accessible presentation remains course and specialist-method instruction.
